assignments.title: Critical Questions: Harriet Hanson Robinson on the Lowell Mills
assignments.html:
MODULE 2 · CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Critical Questions: Harriet Hanson Robinson on the Lowell Mills
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
◆ ◇ ◆
Instructions

Read the primary source for this week: Harriet Hanson Robinson's account of the Lowell mills from Loom and Spindle. Then answer both questions in your own words. Aim for four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. Robinson remembers the mill girls taking pride in earning their own money. What idea about work and independence lies behind that pride, even though she does not name it directly?
  2. Why is a memory written by a mill worker useful to a historian who wants to understand the market revolution? Name one thing it can show that a factory owner's records cannot, and one thing a historian should be careful about when using it.

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

assignments.title: Primary Source Exercise: Finney on Revivals of Religion
assignments.html:
MODULE 2 · PRIMARY SOURCE EXERCISE
Primary Source Exercise: Finney on Revivals of Religion
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
◆ ◇ ◆
Instructions

Read the primary source: an excerpt from Charles Finney's Lectures on Revivals of Religion. Then answer both questions in your own words, in four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. Finney urges people to act now and says that a person who is saved should work to improve society. What idea about human choice lies behind that call, and how is it different from the belief in predestination?
  2. Why would a preacher's belief that people can choose to change matter for American reform movements such as temperance and, later, the fight against slavery?

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

quizzes.title: Intro (Lessons 2.1 and 2.2): How Do New Machines and New Ideas Change Ordinary Lives?
quizzes.description:
MODULE 2 · INTRO QUIZ
Module 2 Intro: How Do New Machines and New Ideas Change Ordinary Lives?
3 questions · survey · one attempt
◆ ◇ ◆
Before you start

Before you start these lessons, answer three quick questions. There are no wrong answers. You will come back to the first question when you finish.

Start with Innovators Bring Industry and Progress to America.

questions.text: Imagine that new machines suddenly let a country make cloth faster and move goods cheaply. How might that change the way ordinary families work, live, and think about right and wrong? Answer in two or three sentences. You will revisit this answer at the end of these lessons.
I have read the goals for these lessons: to explain how machines, canals, and railroads changed Northern life, and how the Second Great Awakening stirred Americans to improve society.

answers.text: Yes, I am ready to begin
Not yet, I have a question

questions.text: This quarter has an optional group capstone. Would you like to work in a group?

answers.text: Yes
No, I will work on my own
Undecided

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: Lessons 2.1 and 2.2
quizzes.description:
MODULE 2 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: Innovators Bring Industry and Progress to America and Preachers Enlarge America’s Conscience
7 questions · 7 points · 2 attempts
◆ ◇ ◆
Before you start

This quiz covers Innovators Bring Industry and Progress to America and Preachers Enlarge America’s Conscience. You may take it twice, and your higher score counts. Some questions ask you to put two or more facts together, so think before you answer.

questions.text: Samuel Slater built a cotton mill in Rhode Island without carrying any plans from Britain. What fact explains why he had to rely on his memory?

answers.text: He could not read English.
He worked as a farmer, not as a mill worker.
Rhode Island merchants refused to buy British plans.
British law forbade sending out plans of the machines and forbade skilled workers to leave.

questions.text: Before the Erie Canal, shipping a ton of freight from Buffalo to New York City cost about $100. After it, the cost was about $10. Which result would you most expect?

answers.text: Farmers in the West would stop selling their crops to the East.
Towns along the route, such as Rochester and Buffalo, would grow, and New York City would become a great port.
New York would sell the canal to the federal government.
Railroads would be built only in the South.

questions.text: John Deere's steel plow helped settle the Midwest. Why did it appeal to people who wanted to own land rather than work in a factory?

answers.text: It was cheaper than any hand tool, so factory owners gave it to workers.
It was made only in Southern factories and sold to Northern farmers.
It could cut the sticky prairie soil, so a family could farm its own land and sell its crops.
It replaced the need for farmers to own any land.

questions.text: Which statement best describes the experience of the young women who worked in the Lowell mills?

answers.text: They earned cash wages, many for the first time, but worked long hours in noisy rooms and struck when pay was cut.
They were paid in company goods and never held cash.
They worked short days but were not allowed to leave the town.
They had no rules to follow and lived wherever they liked.

questions.text: Charles Finney taught that every person could choose to turn to God and that a saved person should work to improve society. How does this connect to the reform societies of the 1830s?

answers.text: It taught that nothing in society could be changed.
It encouraged people to leave the country.
It told people to wait for God to decide who would be saved.
It gave people a reason to join groups that tried to fix problems such as drinking and a lack of schools.

questions.text: A town has no school for its children and a problem with drunkenness. According to the habit Tocqueville noticed, what would Americans most likely do?

answers.text: Wait for the national government to send help.
Form a voluntary society to work on the problem together.
Ask Britain for money.
Pass a law at the Constitutional Convention.

questions.text: Lowell's mills ran on cotton grown in the South. What does this show about the North and South in the 1830s?

answers.text: The South depended on Northern cotton.
Southern planters refused to sell to Northern mills.
The sections were growing into different economies, yet they were still tied together.
Northern mills used only cotton grown by free farmers.

quizzes.title: Outro (Lessons 2.1 and 2.2): Looking Back at Machines and Conscience
quizzes.description:
MODULE 2 · OUTRO QUIZ
Module 2 Outro: Looking Back at Machines and Conscience
4 questions · survey · one attempt
◆ ◇ ◆
Before you start

You have finished these lessons and their work. Answer four short questions. Your answers help your teacher see where students feel strong and where more help is needed.

questions.text: At the start you answered this question: how might new machines and cheaper shipping change the way ordinary families work, live, and think about right and wrong? Answer it again now in two or three sentences. If your answer changed, say what changed it.
How confident do you feel explaining what the transportation revolution was and why it mattered?

answers.text: 1 - Not at all confident
2 - A little confident
3 - Somewhat confident
4 - Mostly confident
5 - Very confident

questions.text: Which idea from these lessons is still unclear to you? It might be the market revolution, interchangeable parts, the Second Great Awakening, predestination, or voluntary societies. Say what you do not yet understand.

When owners cut their pay, the Lowell women went on strike, even though they could lose their jobs. Which of these virtues did that choice require: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, or responsibility? Explain in two or three sentences, and tell about a time you needed that same virtue.

discussions.title: Discussion: Lowell Mills, Opportunity or Exploitation?
discussions.html:
MODULE 2 · DISCUSSION
Discussion: Lowell Mills, Opportunity or Exploitation?
10 points · written post and one reply · threaded discussion
◆ ◇ ◆
The prompt

The Lowell mills gave young farm women wages of their own, a place to live, and a chance to leave the farm. They also meant twelve or thirteen hour days, loud machines, and lint-filled air. Make one specific claim: were the Lowell mills mainly an opportunity, mainly exploitation, or both? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.
